passage:
"I don't read the news any more," Kavitha said, pushing her plate away. "Every channel lied about the flood numbers. Every single one."
"So you believe nothing now?" Ayesha asked.
"Correct. Nothing."
"Then a forward saying the tap water is poisoned is as true as the newspaper?"
"No, but..." Kavitha stopped. "Fine. That's different."
"Not by much. If you trust nothing, whoever shouts loudest steers you, same as if you trusted everything."
Kavitha tore a piece of roti. "Okay. Which ones would you keep?"
"The ones that print corrections when they get it wrong. The local daily does. That bulletin on the radio does too."
"Two sources," Kavitha said. "And I decide slowly."
"Slowly is fine. Nobody needs certainty by dinner 🙂"

qa.q: Which two sources did Ayesha say print corrections?
qa.a: Ayesha named the local daily and the bulletin on the radio.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha say no news could be trusted any more?
qa.a: Kavitha felt that every channel lied about the flood numbers, so trust in all of them collapsed.

qa.q: How can Kavitha handle a new headline under the new plan?
qa.a: Look at the two sources that print corrections, decide slowly and hold the conclusion loosely until more is known.

qa.q: How does Ayesha see trusting no news at all?
qa.a: Ayesha sees it as another way to be steered, because whoever shouts loudest would win, just as with blind trust.

grounding: After repeated lies, total distrust of news is as manipulable as blind trust; a few sources with track records of corrections and loosely held conclusions.

passage:
"Why are you even reading that?" Tushar said, nodding at Minakshi's newspaper. "It's all lies."

"All of it?"

"Every channel, every paper. They lied about the dam, they lied about the flood numbers. I don't believe anything now."

Minakshi folded the paper. "So where do you get news?"

"I don't. Well, I watch a few independent guys online."

"The one who said the moon landing was fake?"

Tushar shifted. "He's not wrong about everything."

"Tushar, you trust him because he says everyone else lies. That's still trusting someone." She tapped the page. "This paper printed a correction on the flood numbers last month. Front page. The guy online never corrects anything."

He was quiet. "So what, I trust everything again?"

"No. Pick three that admit mistakes. Read them. And hold what they say loosely."

He picked up the paper. "Show me the correction."

qa.q: What did the paper Minakshi reads print last month?
qa.a: A correction on the flood numbers, on the front page.

qa.q: What does Tushar's shifting in his seat suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt uncomfortable and a bit defensive when Minakshi pointed out his online source's claim.

qa.q: What did Minakshi suggest instead of believing nothing?
qa.a: Keeping a small set of sources that admit mistakes, reading them, and holding conclusions loosely.

qa.q: How does Minakshi see Tushar's total distrust?
qa.a: Minakshi sees it as just another kind of trust, placed in someone who claims everyone else lies.

grounding: The dialogue shows someone who, after being lied to, trusts no news at all, and learns that total distrust is also manipulable and that a few sources with correction records help.

passage:
I'm Deepika, and for about a year after the election I stopped believing any news at all.

It began honestly. I'd caught three channels lying about the same protest my cousin was at. After that, everything felt fake. I told myself I was being smart.

What I didn't notice was that I'd started believing a set of anonymous accounts, because they agreed with me that everyone else was lying. When one of them said the new vaccine drive was a trick, I nearly stopped my grandmother from going.

My friend Ishita, who works as a fact-checker, sat me down. "You don't trust anyone," she said, "so anyone can fool you."

She showed me how to spot outlets that publish corrections, and I picked three. I read them slowly, and I say "I think" a lot more than I used to.

Grandmother got her vaccine. I'm less certain about everything now, and somehow that feels safer.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel about distrusting all news at first?
qa.a: Deepika felt clever and justified, sure that distrusting everything was the smart choice.

qa.q: What helped Deepika move away from total distrust?
qa.a: Ishita's warning and learning to pick three outlets that publish corrections, while holding conclusions loosely.

qa.q: How might Deepika's grandmother have been affected if Deepika had not changed?
qa.a: She might have missed her vaccine because of a false claim from an anonymous account.

grounding: The reflective account shows someone who, after being lied to, trusted no news, found that total distrust made them easy to fool, and chose a few sources with correction records.
